[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// Options for [`Demangle::demangle`].
[74](https://docs.rs#74)///
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// One can chose from complete, or name-only demangling, and toggle specific demangling features
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// explicitly.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)///
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// The resulting output depends very much on the language of the mangled [`Name`], and may change
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// over time as more fine grained demangling options and features are added. Not all options are
[80](https://docs.rs#80)/// fully supported by each language, and not every feature is mutually exclusive on all languages.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)///
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// # Examples
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// ```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// # #[cfg(feature = "swift")] {
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// use symbolic_common::{Name, NameMangling, Language};
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// let symbol = Name::new("$s8mangling12GenericUnionO3FooyACyxGSicAEmlF", NameMangling::Mangled, Language::Swift);
[90](https://docs.rs#90)///
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// let simple = symbol.demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()).unwrap();
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// assert_eq!(&simple, "GenericUnion.Foo<A>");
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// let full = symbol.demangle(DemangleOptions::complete()).unwrap();
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// assert_eq!(&full, "mangling.GenericUnion.Foo<A>(mangling.GenericUnion<A>.Type) -> (Swift.Int) -> mangling.GenericUnion<A>");
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// # }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// ```
[98](https://docs.rs#98)///

[143](https://docs.rs#143)        || ident.starts_with("___Z")

[149](https://docs.rs#149)}
[150](https://docs.rs#150)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// An MD5 mangled name consists of the prefix "??@", 32 hex digits,
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// and the suffix "@".
[153](https://docs.rs#153)fn is_maybe_md5(ident: &str) -> bool {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    if ident.len() != 36 {
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        return false;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    }
[157](https://docs.rs#157)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    ident.starts_with("??@")
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        && ident.ends_with('@')
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        && ident[3..35].chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_hexdigit())
[161](https://docs.rs#161)}
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)#[cfg(feature = "swift")]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)fn is_maybe_swift(ident: &str) -> bool {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    CString::new(ident)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        .map(|cstr| unsafe { symbolic_demangle_is_swift_symbol(cstr.as_ptr()) != 0 })
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        .unwrap_or(false)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)}
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)#[cfg(not(feature = "swift"))]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)fn is_maybe_swift(_ident: &str) -> bool {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    false
[173](https://docs.rs#173)}

[175](https://docs.rs#175)#[cfg(feature = "msvc")]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)fn try_demangle_msvc(ident: &str, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Option<String> {
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    use msvc_demangler::DemangleFlags as MsvcFlags;
[178](https://docs.rs#178)
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    // the flags are bitflags
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    let mut flags = MsvcFlags::COMPLETE
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        | MsvcFlags::SPACE_AFTER_COMMA
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        | MsvcFlags::HUG_TYPE
[183](https://docs.rs#183)        | MsvcFlags::NO_MS_KEYWORDS
[184](https://docs.rs#184)        | MsvcFlags::NO_CLASS_TYPE;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    if !opts.return_type {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)        flags |= MsvcFlags::NO_FUNCTION_RETURNS;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    if !opts.parameters {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        // a `NO_ARGUMENTS` flag is there in the code, but commented out
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        flags |= MsvcFlags::NAME_ONLY;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    }
[192](https://docs.rs#192)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    msvc_demangler::demangle(ident, flags, Some(MSVC_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH)).ok()
[194](https://docs.rs#194)}
[195](https://docs.rs#195)
[196](https://docs.rs#196)#[cfg(not(feature = "msvc"))]
[197](https://docs.rs#197)fn try_demangle_msvc(_ident: &str, _opts: DemangleOptions) -> Option<String> {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    None
[199](https://docs.rs#199)}
[200](https://docs.rs#200)
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// Removes a suffix consisting of $ followed by 32 hex digits, if there is one,
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// otherwise returns its input.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)fn strip_hash_suffix(ident: &str) -> &str {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    let len = ident.len();
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    if len >= 33 {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)        let mut char_iter = ident.char_indices();
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        while let Some((pos, c)) = char_iter.next_back() {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)            if (len - pos) == 33 && c == '$' {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)                // If we have not yet returned we have a valid suffix to strip.  This is
[210](https://docs.rs#210)                // safe because we know the current pos is on the start of the '$' char
[211](https://docs.rs#211)                // boundary.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)                return &ident[..pos];
[213](https://docs.rs#213)            } else if (len - pos) > 33 || !c.is_ascii_hexdigit() {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)                // If pos is more than 33 bytes from the end a multibyte char made us skip
[215](https://docs.rs#215)                // pos 33, multibyte chars are not hexdigit or $ so nothing to strip.
[216](https://docs.rs#216)                return ident;
[217](https://docs.rs#217)            }
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    }
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ident
[221](https://docs.rs#221)}
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)struct BoundedString {
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    str: String,
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    bound: usize,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)}
[227](https://docs.rs#227)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)impl BoundedString {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    fn new(bound: usize) -> Self {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        Self {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            str: String::new(),
[232](https://docs.rs#232)            bound,
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    }
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    pub fn into_inner(self) -> String {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        self.str
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)}
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)impl std::fmt::Write for BoundedString {
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    fn write_str(&mut self, s: &str) -> std::fmt::Result {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        if self.str.len().saturating_add(s.len()) > self.bound {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            return Err(std::fmt::Error);
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        self.str.write_str(s)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)}
[249](https://docs.rs#249)
[250](https://docs.rs#250)fn try_demangle_cpp(ident: &str, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Option<String> {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    if is_maybe_msvc(ident) {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        return try_demangle_msvc(ident, opts);
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    // C++ *symbols* will always start with a `_Z` prefix, but `cpp_demangle` is a bit more lenient
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    // and will also demangle bare types, turning `a` into `signed char` for example. So lets be
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    // a bit stricter and make sure we always have a `_Z` prefix.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    if !is_maybe_cpp(ident) {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        return None;
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    #[cfg(feature = "cpp")]
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        use cpp_demangle::{DemangleOptions as CppOptions, ParseOptions, Symbol as CppSymbol};
[265](https://docs.rs#265)
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        let stripped = strip_hash_suffix(ident);
[267](https://docs.rs#267)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        let parse_options = ParseOptions::default().recursion_limit(160); // default is 96
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        let symbol = match CppSymbol::new_with_options(stripped, &parse_options) {
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            Ok(symbol) => symbol,
[271](https://docs.rs#271)            Err(_) => return None,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        };
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        let mut cpp_options = CppOptions::new().recursion_limit(192); // default is 128
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        if !opts.parameters {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)            cpp_options = cpp_options.no_params();
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        }
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        if !opts.return_type {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)            cpp_options = cpp_options.no_return_type();
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        }
[281](https://docs.rs#281)
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        // Bound the maximum output string, as a huge number of substitutions could potentially
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        // lead to a "Billion laughs attack".
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        let mut buf = BoundedString::new(4096);
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        symbol
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            .structured_demangle(&mut buf, &cpp_options)
[288](https://docs.rs#288)            .ok()
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            .map(|_| buf.into_inner())
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    #[cfg(not(feature = "cpp"))]
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    {
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        None
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    }
[295](https://docs.rs#295)}
[296](https://docs.rs#296)

[311](https://docs.rs#311)fn try_demangle_swift(ident: &str, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Option<String> {
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    let mut buf = vec![0; 4096];
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    let sym = match CString::new(ident) {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        Ok(sym) => sym,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        Err(_) => return None,
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    };
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    let mut features = 0;
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    if opts.return_type {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        features |= SYMBOLIC_SWIFT_FEATURE_RETURN_TYPE;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    if opts.parameters {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        features |= SYMBOLIC_SWIFT_FEATURE_PARAMETERS;
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    unsafe {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        match symbolic_demangle_swift(sym.as_ptr(), buf.as_mut_ptr(), buf.len(), features) {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)            0 => None,
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            _ => Some(CStr::from_ptr(buf.as_ptr()).to_string_lossy().to_string()),
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }

[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// An extension trait on `Name` for demangling names.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)///
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// See the [module level documentation] for a list of supported languages.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)///
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// [module level documentation]: index.html
[358](https://docs.rs#358)pub trait Demangle {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// Infers the language of a mangled name.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    ///
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// In case the symbol is not mangled or its language is unknown, the return value will be
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// `Language::Unknown`. If the language of the symbol was specified explicitly, this is
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// returned instead. For a list of supported languages, see the [module level documentation].
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    ///
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// # Examples
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    ///
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// ```
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// use symbolic_common::{Language, Name};
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// assert_eq!(Name::from("_ZN3foo3barEv").detect_language(), Language::Cpp);
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// assert_eq!(Name::from("unknown").detect_language(), Language::Unknown);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// ```
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    ///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// [module level documentation]: index.html
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    fn detect_language(&self) -> Language;
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// Demangles the name with the given options.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    ///
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// Returns `None` in one of the following cases:
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    ///  1. The language cannot be detected.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    ///  2. The language is not supported.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    ///  3. Demangling of the name failed.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    ///
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// # Examples
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// ```
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// # #[cfg(feature = "cpp")] {
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// use symbolic_common::Name;
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    ///
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// assert_eq!(
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///     Name::from("_ZN3foo3barEv").demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///     Some("foo::bar".to_string())
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// );
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// assert_eq!(
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///     Name::from("unknown").demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///     None
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// );
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// # }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// ```
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    fn demangle(&self, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Option<String>;
[403](https://docs.rs#403)
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// Tries to demangle the name and falls back to the original name.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// Similar to [`demangle`], except that it returns a borrowed instance of the original name if
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// the name cannot be demangled.
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    ///
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// # Examples
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    ///
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// ```
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// # #[cfg(feature = "cpp")] {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// use symbolic_common::Name;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// assert_eq!(
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///     Name::from("_ZN3foo3barEv").try_demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///     "foo::bar"
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// );
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// assert_eq!(
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    ///     Name::from("unknown").try_demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///     "unknown"
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// );
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// # }
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// ```
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    ///
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    /// [`demangle`]: trait.Demangle.html#tymethod.demangle
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    fn try_demangle(&self, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Cow<'_, str>;
[429](https://docs.rs#429)}
[430](https://docs.rs#430)
[431](https://docs.rs#431)impl Demangle for Name<'_> {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    fn detect_language(&self) -> Language {
[433](https://docs.rs#433)        if self.language() != Language::Unknown {
[434](https://docs.rs#434)            return self.language();
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        }
[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        if is_maybe_objc(self.as_str()) {
[438](https://docs.rs#438)            return Language::ObjC;
[439](https://docs.rs#439)        }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        #[cfg(feature = "rust")]
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        {
[443](https://docs.rs#443)            if rustc_demangle::try_demangle(self.as_str()).is_ok() {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)                return Language::Rust;
[445](https://docs.rs#445)            }
[446](https://docs.rs#446)        }
[447](https://docs.rs#447)
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        if is_maybe_cpp(self.as_str()) || is_maybe_msvc(self.as_str()) {
[449](https://docs.rs#449)            return Language::Cpp;
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        }
[451](https://docs.rs#451)
[452](https://docs.rs#452)        if is_maybe_swift(self.as_str()) {
[453](https://docs.rs#453)            return Language::Swift;
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        }
[455](https://docs.rs#455)
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        Language::Unknown
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    }
[458](https://docs.rs#458)
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    fn demangle(&self, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Option<String> {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        if matches!(self.mangling(), NameMangling::Unmangled) || is_maybe_md5(self.as_str()) {
[461](https://docs.rs#461)            return Some(self.to_string());
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        }
[463](https://docs.rs#463)
[464](https://docs.rs#464)        match self.detect_language() {
[465](https://docs.rs#465)            Language::ObjC => Some(demangle_objc(self.as_str(), opts)),
[466](https://docs.rs#466)            Language::ObjCpp => try_demangle_objcpp(self.as_str(), opts),
[467](https://docs.rs#467)            Language::Rust => try_demangle_rust(self.as_str(), opts),
[468](https://docs.rs#468)            Language::Cpp => try_demangle_cpp(self.as_str(), opts),
[469](https://docs.rs#469)            Language::Swift => try_demangle_swift(self.as_str(), opts),
[470](https://docs.rs#470)            _ => None,
[471](https://docs.rs#471)        }
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    }
[473](https://docs.rs#473)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    fn try_demangle(&self, opts: DemangleOptions) -> Cow<'_, str> {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        if matches!(self.mangling(), NameMangling::Unmangled) {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            return Cow::Borrowed(self.as_str());
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        }
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        match self.demangle(opts) {
[479](https://docs.rs#479)            Some(demangled) => Cow::Owned(demangled),
[480](https://docs.rs#480)            None => Cow::Borrowed(self.as_str()),
[481](https://docs.rs#481)        }
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)}
[484](https://docs.rs#484)
[485](https://docs.rs#485)/// Demangles an identifier and falls back to the original symbol.
[486](https://docs.rs#486)///
[487](https://docs.rs#487)/// This is a shortcut for [`Demangle::try_demangle`] with complete demangling.
[488](https://docs.rs#488)///
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// # Examples
[490](https://docs.rs#490)///
[491](https://docs.rs#491)/// ```
[492](https://docs.rs#492)/// # #[cfg(feature = "cpp")] {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)/// assert_eq!(symbolic_demangle::demangle("_ZN3foo3barEv"), "foo::bar()");
[494](https://docs.rs#494)/// # }
[495](https://docs.rs#495)/// ```
[496](https://docs.rs#496)///
[497](https://docs.rs#497)/// [`Demangle::try_demangle`]: trait.Demangle.html#tymethod.try_demangle
[498](https://docs.rs#498)pub fn demangle(ident: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> {
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    match Name::from(ident).demangle(DemangleOptions::complete()) {
[500](https://docs.rs#500)        Some(demangled) => Cow::Owned(demangled),
[501](https://docs.rs#501)        None => Cow::Borrowed(ident),
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    }
[503](https://docs.rs#503)}

# DemangleOptions in symbolic_demangle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/symbolic-demangle/13.8.0/symbolic_demangle/struct.DemangleOptions.html

`pub struct DemangleOptions { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Options for [ Demangle::demangle](https://docs.rs/trait.Demangle.html#tymethod.demangle).

One can chose from complete, or name-only demangling, and toggle specific demangling features explicitly.

The resulting output depends very much on the language of the mangled [ Name](https://docs.rs/symbolic-common/13.8.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/symbolic_common/types/struct.Name.html), and may change
over time as more fine grained demangling options and features are added. Not all options are
fully supported by each language, and not every feature is mutually exclusive on all languages.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use symbolic_common::{Name, NameMangling, Language};
use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
let symbol = Name::new("$s8mangling12GenericUnionO3FooyACyxGSicAEmlF", NameMangling::Mangled, Language::Swift);
let simple = symbol.demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&simple, "GenericUnion.Foo<A>");
let full = symbol.demangle(DemangleOptions::complete()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(&full, "mangling.GenericUnion.Foo<A>(mangling.GenericUnion<A>.Type) -> (Swift.Int) -> mangling.GenericUnion<A>");
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

DemangleOptions that output the most simple (likely name-only) demangling.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

Infers the language of a mangled name.

In case the symbol is not mangled or its language is unknown, the return value will be
`Language::Unknown`. If the language of the symbol was specified explicitly, this is
returned instead. For a list of supported languages, see the [module level documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html).

use symbolic_common::{Language, Name};
use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
assert_eq!(Name::from("_ZN3foo3barEv").detect_language(), Language::Cpp);
assert_eq!(Name::from("unknown").detect_language(), Language::Unknown);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/symbolic_demangle/lib.rs.html#402)#### fn [demangle](https://docs.rs#tymethod.demangle)(&self, opts: [DemangleOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.DemangleOptions.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/symbolic_demangle/lib.rs.html#402)

#### fn [demangle](https://docs.rs#tymethod.demangle)(&self, opts: [DemangleOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.DemangleOptions.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>

Demangles the name with the given options.

Returns `None` in one of the following cases:

- The language cannot be detected.
- The language is not supported.
- Demangling of the name failed.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use symbolic_common::Name;
use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
assert_eq!(
    Name::from("_ZN3foo3barEv").demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
    Some("foo::bar".to_string())
);
assert_eq!(
    Name::from("unknown").demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
    None
);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/symbolic_demangle/lib.rs.html#428)#### fn [try_demangle](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_demangle)(&self, opts: [DemangleOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.DemangleOptions.html)) -> [Cow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)<'_, [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>

Tries to demangle the name and falls back to the original name.

Similar to [ demangle](https://docs.rs/trait.Demangle.html#tymethod.demangle), except that it returns a borrowed instance of the original name if
the name cannot be demangled.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use symbolic_common::Name;
use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
assert_eq!(
    Name::from("_ZN3foo3barEv").try_demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
    "foo::bar"
);
assert_eq!(
    Name::from("unknown").try_demangle(DemangleOptions::name_only()),
    "unknown"
);
```

# demangle in symbolic_demangle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/symbolic-demangle/13.8.0/symbolic_demangle/fn.demangle.html

## Expand description

Demangles an identifier and falls back to the original symbol.

This is a shortcut for [ Demangle::try_demangle](https://docs.rs/trait.Demangle.html#tymethod.try_demangle) with complete demangling.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

`assert_eq!(symbolic_demangle::demangle("_ZN3foo3barEv"), "foo::bar()");`

---

# symbolic_demangle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/symbolic-demangle/latest/symbolic_demangle/

## Expand description

Demangling support for various languages and compilers.

Currently supported languages are:

- C++ (GCC-style compilers and MSVC) (`features = ["cpp", "msvc"]`)
- Rust (both `legacy`and`v0`) (`features = ["rust"]`)
- Swift (up to Swift 5.3) (`features = ["swift"]`)

As the demangling schemes for the languages are different, the supported demangling features are inconsistent. For example, argument types were not encoded in legacy Rust mangling and thus not available in demangled names. The demangling results should not be considered stable, and may change over time as more demangling features are added.

This module is part of the `symbolic` crate and can be enabled via the `demangle` feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use symbolic_common::{Language, Name};
use symbolic_demangle::{Demangle, DemangleOptions};
let name = Name::from("__ZN3std2io4Read11read_to_end17hb85a0f6802e14499E");
assert_eq!(name.detect_language(), Language::Rust);
assert_eq!(
    name.try_demangle(DemangleOptions::complete()),
    "std::io::Read::read_to_end"
);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Demangle](https://docs.rs/struct.DemangleOptions.html)- Options
- Options for `Demangle::demangle`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Demangle](https://docs.rs/trait.Demangle.html)
- An extension trait on `Name`for demangling names.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [demangle](https://docs.rs/fn.demangle.html)
- Demangles an identifier and falls back to the original symbol.

| Network access | blocked |

                    to get them increased.

# bitflags 2.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bitflags/^2

# bitflags

`bitflags` generates flags enums with well-defined semantics and ergonomic end-user APIs.

You can use `bitflags` to:

- provide more user-friendly bindings to C APIs where flags may or may not be fully known in advance.
- generate efficient options types with string parsing and formatting support.

You can't use `bitflags` to:

-
guarantee only bits corresponding to defined flags will ever be set. `bitflags`allows access to the underlying bits type so arbitrary bits may be set.
-
define bitfields. `bitflags`only generates types where set bits denote the presence of some combination of flags.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.13.0"
```
and this to your source code:

```
use bitflags;
```
## Example

Generate a flags structure:

```
use bitflags;
// The `bitflags!` macro generates `struct`s that manage a set of flags.
bitflags!
```
## Cargo features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

Also see [ bitflags_derive](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags-derive) for other flags-aware traits.

## Rust Version Support

The minimum supported Rust version is documented in the `Cargo.toml` file.
This may be bumped in minor releases as necessary.

# cpp_demangle 0.4.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp_demangle/^0.4.1

`cpp_demangle`: a C++ linker symbol demangler

This crate can parse a C++ “mangled” linker symbol name into a Rust value
describing what the name refers to: a variable, a function, a virtual table,
etc. The description type implements `Display`, producing human-readable text
describing the mangled name. Debuggers and profilers can use this crate to
provide more meaningful output.

C++ requires the compiler to choose names for linker symbols consistently across
compilation units, so that two compilation units that have seen the same
declarations can pair up definitions in one unit with references in another.
Almost all platforms other than Microsoft Windows follow the
[Itanium C++ ABI](https://itanium-cxx-abi.github.io/cxx-abi/abi.html#mangling)'s rules for this.

For example, suppose a C++ compilation unit has the definition:

```
namespace space {
  int foo(int x, int y) { return x+y; }
}
```
The Itanium C++ ABI specifies that the linker symbol for that function must be
named `_ZN5space3fooEii`. This crate can parse that name into a Rust value
representing its structure. Formatting the value with the `format!` macro or the
`std::string::ToString::to_string` trait method yields the string
`space::foo(int, int)`, which is more meaningful to the C++ developer.

## Usage

Add `cpp_demangle` to your crate's `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.4.5"
```
And then demangle some C++ symbols!

```
extern crate cpp_demangle;
use Symbol;
use ToString;
let mangled = b"_ZN5space3fooEibc";
let sym = new
    .expect;
let demangled = sym.to_string;
assert_eq!;
```
`no_std` Support

`cpp_demangle` may be configured for working in `no_std` environments that still
have allocation support via the `alloc` crate. This is nightly rust only, at the
moment, since the `alloc` crate's collections aren't stabilized.

Disable the "std" feature, and enable the "alloc" feature:

```
[]
 = {
  version = "0.4.5",
   = false,
   = ["alloc"]
}
```
## Documentation

Example programs:

-
Install it locally with this command: `cargo install cpp_demangle --example cppfilt`

## Implementation Status

Work is ongoing. While `cpp_demangle` can parse every mangled symbol in
`libiberty`'s demangler's test suite (the canonical Itanium C++ symbol demangler
used by GNU tools such as `c++filt`), it does not format all of them
character-for-character identically. I'm working on fixing that ;)

Despite that, I believe `cpp_demangle` is fairly robust. I've been
running [AFL](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/afl.rs) on `cpp_demangle` overnight and it hasn't found any panics for a
long time now (and never found any crashes -- thanks Rust!).

# itoa 1.0.18 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/itoa/^1.0

# itoa

This crate provides a fast conversion of integer primitives to decimal strings.
The implementation comes straight from [libcore](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.92.0/library/core/src/fmt/num.rs#L190-L253) but avoids the performance
penalty of going through [ core::fmt::Formatter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/struct.Formatter.html).

See also [ zmij](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij) for printing floating point primitives.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Example

```
```
## Performance

The [itoa-benchmark](https://github.com/dtolnay/itoa-benchmark) compares this library and other Rust integer formatting
implementations across a range of integer sizes. The vertical axis in this chart
shows nanoseconds taken by a single execution of
`itoa::Buffer::new().format(value)` so a lower result indicates a faster
library.

# rustc-demangle 0.1.27 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustc-demangle/^0.1.21

# rustc-demangle

Demangling for Rust symbols, written in Rust.

## Usage

You can add this as a dependency via your `Cargo.toml`

```
[]
 = "0.1"
```
and then be sure to check out the [crate
documentation](https://docs.rs/rustc-demangle) for usage.

## Usage from non-Rust languages

You can also use this crate from other languages via the C API wrapper in the
`crates/capi` directory. This can be build with:

```
```
You'll then find `target/release/librustc_demangle.a` and
`target/release/librustc_demangle.so` (or a different name depending on your
platform). These objects implement the interface specified in
`crates/capi/include/rustc_demangle.h`.

If your build system does not support Rust, there is also a mostly-identical
C version in the `crates/native-c` which you can use via copy-paste or as
a git submodule. Read `crates/native-c/README.md` for more details. It is
likely to be less supported than the Rust version, so it is better to use
the Rust version if your build system supports it.

Both the Rust and C versions don't require memory allocation or any other operating-system support.

# cc 1.2.65 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cc/^1.0.79

# cc-rs

A library for
[Cargo build scripts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html)
to compile a set of C/C++/assembly/CUDA files into a static archive for Cargo to
link into the crate being built. This crate does not compile code itself; it
calls out to the default compiler for the platform. This crate will
automatically detect situations such as cross compilation and various
environment variables and will build code appropriately.

Refer to the [documentation](https://docs.rs/cc) for detailed usage
instructions.

As the demangling schemes for the languages are different, the supported demangling features are inconsistent. For example, argument types were not encoded in legacy Rust mangling and thus not available in demangled names.

This module is part of the `symbolic` crate and can be enabled via the `demangle` feature.

## Examples

```
use ;
use ;
let name = new;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

# symbolic-demangle 9.1.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/symbolic-demangle/9.1.3

# symbolic-demangle

Demangling support for various languages and compilers.

Currently supported languages are:

- C++ (GCC-style compilers and MSVC)
- Rust (both `legacy`and`v0`)
- Swift (up to Swift 5.2)

As the demangling schemes for the languages are different, the supported demangling features are inconsistent. For example, argument types were not encoded in legacy Rust mangling and thus not available in demangled names.

This module is part of the `symbolic` crate and can be enabled via the `demangle` feature.

## Examples

```
use ;
use ;
let name = new;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
License: MIT

---

# symbolic-demangle 7.3.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/symbolic-demangle/7.3.3

Provides demangling support.

Currently supported languages:

- C++ (without windows)
- Rust
- Swift

As the demangling schemes for different languages are different, the feature set is also inconsistent. In particular Rust for instance has no overloading so argument types are generally not expected to be encoded into the function name whereas they are in Swift and C++.

## Examples

```
use ;
use Demangle;
let name = new;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

---

# bitflags 2.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bitflags/2.13.0

# bitflags

`bitflags` generates flags enums with well-defined semantics and ergonomic end-user APIs.

You can use `bitflags` to:

- provide more user-friendly bindings to C APIs where flags may or may not be fully known in advance.
- generate efficient options types with string parsing and formatting support.

You can't use `bitflags` to:

-
guarantee only bits corresponding to defined flags will ever be set. `bitflags`allows access to the underlying bits type so arbitrary bits may be set.
-
define bitfields. `bitflags`only generates types where set bits denote the presence of some combination of flags.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.13.0"
```
and this to your source code:

```
use bitflags;
```
## Example

Generate a flags structure:

```
use bitflags;
// The `bitflags!` macro generates `struct`s that manage a set of flags.
bitflags!
```
## Cargo features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

Also see [ bitflags_derive](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags-derive) for other flags-aware traits.

## Rust Version Support

The minimum supported Rust version is documented in the `Cargo.toml` file.
This may be bumped in minor releases as necessary.

---

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arbitrary/^1.0/

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

---

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.12/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use checked::`- [CheckedBitPattern](https://docs.rs/checked/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html);
- `pub use`- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)::*;- `extern_crate_alloc`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)- `extern_crate_alloc`
- Stuff to boost things in the `alloc`crate.
- [checked](https://docs.rs/checked/index.html)
- Checked versions of the casting functions exposed in crate root
that support `CheckedBitPattern`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of.html)- of
- Find the offset in bytes of the given `$field`of`$Type`. Requires an already initialized`$instance`value to work with.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [PodCast](https://docs.rs/enum.PodCastError.html)- Error
- The things that can go wrong when casting between `Pod`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types that are valid for any bit pattern.
- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html)
- A trait indicating that:
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data”.
- [PodIn](https://docs.rs/trait.PodInOption.html)- Option
- Trait for types which are [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/trait.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]`wrapper around the`Inner`value.
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)
- Trait for types that can be safely created with
`zeroed`
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroableInOption.html)- InOption
- Trait for types which are [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of.html)- of
- Re-interprets `&T`as`&[u8]`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of_mut.html)- of_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut T`as`&mut [u8]`.
- [cast](https://docs.rs/fn.cast.html)
- Cast `A`into`B`
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_mut.html)- mut
- Cast `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_ref.html)- ref
- Cast `&A`into`&B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice.html)- slice
- Cast `&[A]`into`&[B]`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice_mut.html)- slice_ - mut
- Cast `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`.
- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `slice`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes.html)- bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes_mut.html)- bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast.html)- cast - `must_cast`
- Cast `A`into`B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref - `must_cast`
- Convert `&A`into`&B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice - `must_cast`
- Convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to.html)- align_ - to
- As `align_to``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to_mut.html)- align_ - to_ - mut
- As `align_to_mut``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_read_unaligned.html)- read_ - unaligned
- Reads the slice into a `T`value.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast.html)- cast
- Try to cast `A`into`B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut
- Try to convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref
- Try to convert a `&A`into`&B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice
- Try to convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut
- Try to convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes.html)- from_ - bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes_mut.html)- from_ - bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_pod_read_unaligned.html)- pod_ - read_ - unaligned
- Reads from the bytes as if they were a `T`.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `target`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [zeroed](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroed.html)- `const_zeroed`
- Same as `Zeroable::zeroed``const fn`const.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/derive.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern - `derive`

- Derive the `Hash`trait for a type
- [Checked](https://docs.rs/derive.CheckedBitPattern.html)- BitPattern - `derive`

- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/derive.Contiguous.html)- `derive`
- Derive the `Contiguous`trait for an enum
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/derive.NoUninit.html)- `derive`
- Derive the `NoUninit`trait for a struct or enum
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/derive.Pod.html)- `derive`
- Derive the `Pod`trait for a struct
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/derive.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper - `derive`
- Derive the `TransparentWrapper`trait for a struct
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/derive.Zeroable.html)- `derive`
- Derive the `Zeroable`trait for a type.

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/^1.0.228/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.12.2/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)::*;- `extern_crate_alloc`

- [checked](https://docs.rs/checked/index.html)

that support `CheckedBitPattern`

- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html)
- A trait indicating that:
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data”.
- [PodIn](https://docs.rs/trait.PodInOption.html)- Option
- Trait for types which are [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/trait.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]`wrapper around the`Inner`value.
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)
- Trait for types that can be safely created with
`zeroed`
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroableInOption.html)- InOption
- Trait for types which are [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast.html)- cast - `must_cast`

- Convert `&A`into`&B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.

- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut - `must_cast`

- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to.html)- align_ - to

- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to_mut.html)- align_ - to_ - mut
- As `align_to_mut``Pod`

- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut

- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut
- Try to convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes.html)- from_ - bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes_mut.html)- from_ - bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_pod_read_unaligned.html)- pod_ - read_ - unaligned

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize JSON data to a Rust data structure.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- When serializing or deserializing JSON goes wrong.
- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- A map of String to serde_json::Value.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)- `std`
- Serialize a Rust data structure into JSON data.
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- The Value enum, a loosely typed way of representing any valid JSON value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [json](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html)
- Construct a `serde_json::Value`from a JSON literal.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)
- A structure that deserializes JSON into Rust values.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- This type represents all possible errors that can occur when serializing or deserializing JSON data.
- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- Represents a JSON key/value type.

- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDeserializer.html)- Deserializer

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.103/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# serde_test - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_test/^1.0.19/

## Expand description

This crate provides a convenient concise way to write unit tests for
implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`The `Serialize` impl for a value can be characterized by the sequence of
[ Serializer](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serializer.html) calls that are made in the course of serializing the value,
so

`serde_test` provides a [abstraction which corresponds roughly to](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)

`Token``Serializer` method calls. There is an [function to test that a value serializes to a particular sequence of method calls, an](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_ser_tokens.html)

`assert_ser_tokens`[function to test that a value can be deserialized from a particular sequence of method calls, and an](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_de_tokens.html)

`assert_de_tokens`[function to test both directions. There are also functions to test expected failure conditions.](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_tokens.html)

`assert_tokens`Here is an example from the [ linked-hash-map](https://github.com/contain-rs/linked-hash-map) crate.

```
use linked_hash_map::LinkedHashMap;
use serde_test::{assert_tokens, Token};
#[test]
fn test_ser_de_empty() {
    let map = LinkedHashMap::<char, u32>::new();
    assert_tokens(
        &map,
        &[
            Token::Map { len: Some(0) },
            Token::MapEnd,
        ],
    );
}
#[test]
fn test_ser_de() {
    let mut map = LinkedHashMap::new();
    map.insert('b', 20);
    map.insert('a', 10);
    map.insert('c', 30);
    assert_tokens(
        &map,
        &[
            Token::Map { len: Some(3) },
            Token::Char('b'),
            Token::I32(20),
            Token::Char('a'),
            Token::I32(10),
            Token::Char('c'),
            Token::I32(30),
            Token::MapEnd,
        ],
    );
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Configure](https://docs.rs/trait.Configure.html)
- Trait to determine whether a value is represented in human-readable or compact form.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_de_tokens.html)- de_ - tokens
- Asserts that the given `tokens`deserialize into`value`.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_de_tokens_error.html)- de_ - tokens_ - error
- Asserts that the given `tokens`yield`error`when deserializing.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_ser_tokens.html)- ser_ - tokens
- Asserts that `value`serializes to the given`tokens`.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_ser_tokens_error.html)- ser_ - tokens_ - error
- Asserts that `value`serializes to the given`tokens`, and then yields`error`.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_tokens.html)- tokens
- Runs both `assert_ser_tokens`and`assert_de_tokens`.
